claim: Retrieving a memory can modify its influence on subsequent behavior.
source: Retrieving a memory can modify its influence on subsequent behavior.
evidence: This is a foundational claim stated in the abstract that frames the entire paper.

claim: Memory modification occurs through classical associative learning.
source: We develop a computational theory of memory modification, according to which modification of a memory trace occurs through classical associative learning, but which memory trace is eligible for modification depends on a structure learning mechanism that discovers the units of association by segmenting the stream of experience into statistically distinct clusters (latent causes).
evidence: This is a core theoretical claim of the model presented in the paper.

claim: Which memory trace is eligible for modification depends on a structure learning mechanism that discovers units of association by segmenting experience into statistically distinct clusters (latent causes).
source: We develop a computational theory of memory modification, according to which modification of a memory trace occurs through classical associative learning, but which memory trace is eligible for modification depends on a structure learning mechanism that discovers the units of association by segmenting the stream of experience into statistically distinct clusters (latent causes).
evidence: This is a core theoretical claim of the model presented in the paper.

claim: New memories are formed when the structure learning mechanism infers that a new latent cause underlies current sensory observations.
source: New memories are formed when the structure learning mechanism infers that a new latent cause underlies current sensory observations.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: Old memories are modified when old and new sensory observations are inferred to have been generated by the same latent cause.
source: By the same token, old memories are modified when old and new sensory observations are inferred to have been generated by the same latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: The model can reproduce the major experimental findings from studies of memory modification in the Pavlovian conditioning literature.
source: Simulations demonstrate that our model can reproduce the major experimental findings from studies of memory modification in the Pavlovian conditioning literature.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented throughout the paper.

claim: Memory retrieval is a significant learning event in both humans and animals.
source: In both humans and animals, memory retrieval is a significant learning event (Dudai, 2012; Roediger and Butler, 2011; Spear, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A memory's strength and content can be modified immediately after retrieval.
source: A memory's strength and content can be modified immediately after retrieval, and this malleability is often more potent than new learning without retrieval.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from the literature.

claim: Post-retrieval memory malleability is often more potent than new learning without retrieval.
source: A memory's strength and content can be modified immediately after retrieval, and this malleability is often more potent than new learning without retrieval.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from the literature.

claim: Decisions about when to modify an old memory or form a new memory are guided by inferences about the latent causes of sensory data.
source: Central to our theory is the idea that memory is inferential in nature: Decisions about when to modify an old memory or form a new memory are guided by inferences about the latent causes of sensory data (Gershman et al., 2010, 2014, 2015).
evidence: This is a core theoretical claim of the model, building on prior work.

claim: Memories contain statistical information about inferred latent causes.
source: Memories contain statistical information about inferred latent causes (when they are likely to occur, what sensory data they tend to generate).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the content of memories in the model.

claim: Memory statistics are retrieved and updated whenever a previously inferred latent cause is believed to have generated new sensory data.
source: These statistics are retrieved and updated whenever a previously inferred latent cause is believed to have generated new sensory data.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the dynamics of memory updating in the model.

claim: Conditions that promote the retrieval of a memory are the conditions that promote the inference that the same previously inferred latent cause is once again active.
source: Conditions that promote the retrieval of a memory are, according to this account, precisely the conditions that promote the inference that the same previously inferred latent cause is once again active.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim linking retrieval to latent cause inference.

claim: If no previously inferred latent cause adequately predicts the current sensory data, then a new memory is formed.
source: If no previously inferred latent cause adequately predicts the current sensory data, then a new memory is formed.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: Memory modification is intimately connected to the process of latent structure learning.
source: Thus, memory modification is intimately connected to the process of latent structure learning.
evidence: This is a core theoretical claim of the model.

claim: Misanin et al. (1968) found that electroconvulsive shock had no effect on a fear memory acquired a day previously.
source: In a classic experiment using a Pavlovian fear conditioning task, Misanin et al. (1968) found that electroconvulsive shock had no effect on a fear memory acquired a day previously; however, if the animal was briefly reexposed to the acquisition cue prior to electroconvulsive shock, the animal subsequently exhibited loss of fear.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: If an animal was briefly reexposed to the acquisition cue prior to electroconvulsive shock, the animal subsequently exhibited loss of fear.
source: In a classic experiment using a Pavlovian fear conditioning task, Misanin et al. (1968) found that electroconvulsive shock had no effect on a fear memory acquired a day previously; however, if the animal was briefly reexposed to the acquisition cue prior to electroconvulsive shock, the animal subsequently exhibited loss of fear.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Nader et al. (2000) showed that retrograde amnesia for an acquired fear memory could be produced by injection of a protein synthesis inhibitor into the lateral nucleus of the amygdala shortly after reexposure to the acquisition cue.
source: Contemporary neuroscientific interest in this phenomenon was ignited by Nader et al. (2000), who showed that retrograde amnesia for an acquired fear memory could be produced by injection of a protein synthesis inhibitor (PSI) into the lateral nucleus of the amygdala shortly after reexposure to the acquisition cue.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Stronger and older memories are harder to modify following retrieval.
source: For instance, it has been shown that stronger and older memories are harder to modify following retrieval (Suzuki et al., 2004), and that the modification is cue-specific (Doyère et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from cited studies.

claim: Memory modification is cue-specific.
source: For instance, it has been shown that stronger and older memories are harder to modify following retrieval (Suzuki et al., 2004), and that the modification is cue-specific (Doyère et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Memory modification can be obtained with a purely behavioral procedure.
source: Importantly, there is now evidence that memory modification can be obtained with a purely behavioral procedure.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from the literature.

claim: Monfils et al. (2009) and Schiller et al. (2010) showed that reexposing a subject to the cue shortly (10 min to 1 hr) before extinction training is sufficient to reduce conditioned responding at test in rats and humans.
source: In particular, Monfils et al. (2009) and Schiller et al. (2010) showed, in rats and in humans, that reexposing a subject to the cue shortly (10 min to 1 hr) before extinction training is sufficient to reduce conditioned responding at test.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from cited studies.

claim: The Rescorla-Wagner model predicts that extinction is unlearning.
source: The main weakness of the Rescorla-Wagner model, and many similar models (Pearce and Bouton, 2001), is its prediction that presenting the CS repeatedly by itself ('extinction') will erase the CS-US association formed during acquisition—in other words, the model predicts that extinction is unlearning.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the Rescorla-Wagner model.

claim: The assumption that extinction is unlearning is wrong.
source: It is widely accepted that this assumption, shared by a large class of models, is wrong (Delamater, 2004; Dunsmoor et al., 2015; Gallistel, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about the consensus in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Simply increasing the time between extinction and test is sufficient to increase responding to the extinguished CS, a phenomenon known as spontaneous recovery.
source: For example, simply increasing the time between extinction and test is sufficient to increase responding to the extinguished CS, a phenomenon known as spontaneous recovery (Pavlov, 1927; Rescorla, 2004).
evidence: This is an empirical phenomenon from the literature.

claim: Reexposure to the US alone prior to test increases conditioned responding to the CS, a phenomenon known as reinstatement.
source: Another example is reinstatement: reexposure to the US alone prior to test increases conditioned responding to the CS (Bouton and Bolles, 1979b; Pavlov, 1927; Rescorla and Heth, 1975).
evidence: This is an empirical phenomenon from the literature.

claim: Conditioned responding can be recovered if the animal is returned to the acquisition context, a phenomenon known as renewal.
source: Conditioned responding can also be recovered if the animal is returned to the acquisition context, a phenomenon known as renewal (Bouton and Bolles, 1979a).
evidence: This is an empirical phenomenon from the literature.

claim: Bouton (1993) interpreted the attenuation of responding after extinction in terms of the formation of an extinction memory that competes for retrieval with the acquisition memory.
source: Bouton (1993) interpreted the attenuation of responding after extinction in terms of the formation of an extinction memory that competes for retrieval with the acquisition memory; this retroactive interference can be relieved by a change in temporal context or the presence of retrieval cues, thereby leading to recovery of the original CS (see also Miller and Laborda, 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation from a cited study.

claim: The latent cause theory treats context as the input into a structure learning system, which outputs a parse of experience into latent causes.
source: In this section, we develop a latent cause theory of Pavlovian conditioning that treats context (operationalized as the history of sensory data) as the input into a structure learning system, which outputs a parse of experience into latent causes—hypothetical entities in the environment that govern the distribution of stimulus configurations (Courville, 2006; Courville et al., 2006; Gershman et al., 2010; Gershman and Niv, 2012; Gershman et al., 2013a, 2015; Soto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a core theoretical claim of the model, building on prior work.

claim: New causes are inferred when existing causes fail to accurately predict the currently observed CS-US contingency.
source: New causes are inferred when existing causes fail to accurately predict the currently observed CS-US contingency (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Memory modification arises when CS reexposure provides evidence to the animal that the latent cause assigned to the acquisition phase is once again active, making that cause's associations eligible for updating.
source: Memory modification arises when CS reexposure provides evidence to the animal that the latent cause assigned to the acquisition phase is once again active, making that cause's associations eligible for updating (or disruption by amnestic agents like PSIs).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the mechanism of memory modification in the model.

claim: The theory consists of two interacting sub-systems: an associative-learning system and a structure learning system.
source: The theory consists of two interacting sub-systems (Figure 1C): an associative-learning system updates a set of CS-US associations using a delta rule (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Sutton and Barto, 1998; Widrow and Hoff, 1960), while a structure learning system updates an approximation of the posterior distribution over latent causes using Bayes' rule.
evidence: This is a core theoretical claim about the model architecture, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The associative-learning system updates a set of CS-US associations using a delta rule.
source: The theory consists of two interacting sub-systems (Figure 1C): an associative-learning system updates a set of CS-US associations using a delta rule (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Sutton and Barto, 1998; Widrow and Hoff, 1960), while a structure learning system updates an approximation of the posterior distribution over latent causes using Bayes' rule.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the associative learning component, with citations to prior work.

claim: The structure learning system updates an approximation of the posterior distribution over latent causes using Bayes' rule.
source: The theory consists of two interacting sub-systems (Figure 1C): an associative-learning system updates a set of CS-US associations using a delta rule (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Sutton and Barto, 1998; Widrow and Hoff, 1960), while a structure learning system updates an approximation of the posterior distribution over latent causes using Bayes' rule.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the structure learning component.

claim: The associative learning system can maintain multiple sets of associations between any CS-US pair (one for each latent cause).
source: It is useful to envision the associative-learning system as almost identical to the Rescorla-Wagner model, with the key difference that the system can maintain multiple sets of associations between any CS-US pair (one for each latent cause; Figure 1B) instead of just a single set.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the model architecture, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The multiple associations are combined into a single prediction of the US by averaging the US prediction for each cause, weighted by the posterior probability of that cause being active.
source: Given a particular CS configuration (e.g., tone in a red box), the multiple associations are combined into a single prediction of the US by averaging the US prediction for each cause, weighted by the posterior probability of that cause being active.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how predictions are computed in the model.

claim: In the special case that only a single latent cause is inferred by the structure learning system, the associative learning system's computations are almost identical to the Rescorla-Wagner model.
source: In the special case that only a single latent cause is inferred by the structure learning system, the associative learning system's computations are almost identical to the Rescorla-Wagner model (see the Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the relationship between the model and the Rescorla-Wagner model.

claim: A single latent cause is responsible for all the events (CSs and USs) in any given trial.
source: Finally, according to the animal's internal model, a single latent cause is responsible for all the events (CSs and USs) in any given trial.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption of the model.

claim: The power law kernel has a temporal compression property: as two timepoints both recede into the past relative to a third timepoint, they become almost equally distant from it.
source: However, this advantage diminishes over time, and asymptotically disappears: as t1 and t2 both recede into the past relative to t3, they become (almost) equally distant from t3, and it is equally likely that one of their causes also caused t3.
evidence: This is a theoretical property of the power law kernel, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The EM algorithm alternates between structure learning (E-step) and associative learning (M-step).
source: For our model, the EM algorithm takes the following form (see Materials and methods for a derivation): after each observation, the model alternates between structure learning (the E-step, in which the posterior distribution over latent causes is updated assuming the current weights associated with the different causes are the true weights) and associative learning (the M-step, in which the weights for each cause are updated using a delta rule, conditional on the posterior over latent causes).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the learning algorithm.

claim: Associative learning in the model is a generalization of the Rescorla-Wagner model.
source: Associative learning in our model (the M-step of the EM algorithm) is a generalization of the Rescorla-Wagner model (see the Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the relationship between the model and the Rescorla-Wagner model.

claim: The transition from acquisition to extinction involves a dramatic change in the statistics of the animal's sensory inputs, leading the animal to assign acquisition and extinction trials to different latent causes.
source: In previous work (Gershman et al., 2010), we argued that the transition from acquisition to extinction involves a dramatic change in the statistics of the animal's sensory inputs, leading the animal to assign acquisition and extinction trials to different latent causes.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from prior work, cited here.

claim: The result of partitioning acquisition and extinction into different latent causes is that the acquisition associations are not unlearned during extinction, and hence can be later recovered.
source: The result of this partitioning is that the acquisition associations are not unlearned during extinction, and hence can be later recovered, as is observed experimentally (Bouton, 2004).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that matches empirical observations.

claim: The key to persistent reduction in fear is to finesse the animal's sensory statistics such that the posterior distribution over latent causes favors assigning both acquisition and extinction phases to the same latent cause.
source: Thus, according to our model, the key to persistent reduction in fear is to finesse the animal's sensory statistics such that the posterior distribution over latent causes favors assigning both acquisition and extinction phases to the same latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: The prediction error plays two roles in the model: it is an associative learning signal and a segmentation signal indicating when a new latent cause is active.
source: The prediction error plays two roles in our model: it is an associative learning signal that teaches the animal how to adjust its associative weights, and it is a segmentation signal indicating when a new latent cause is active.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the dual role of prediction error in the model.

claim: The prediction error can be reduced in two different ways: either by associative learning or by structure learning.
source: In our model, however, the prediction error can be reduced in two different ways: either by associative learning (e.g., unlearning the CS-US association) or by structure learning (e.g., assigning the extinction trials to a new latent cause).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how the model handles prediction errors.

claim: Initially, the prior simplicity bias towards a small number of latent causes favors unlearning, but persistent accumulation of prediction errors over the course of extinction eventually makes the posterior probability of a new cause high.
source: Initially, the prior simplicity bias towards a small number of latent causes favors unlearning, but persistent accumulation of these prediction errors over the course of extinction eventually makes the posterior probability of a new cause high.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the dynamics of structure learning during extinction.

claim: There should exist an intermediate 'sweet spot' for extinction learning where the prediction errors are large enough to induce considerable weight change but small enough to avoid inferring a new latent cause.
source: In theory, therefore, there should exist an intermediate 'sweet spot' for extinction learning where the prediction errors are large enough to induce considerable weight change but small enough to avoid inferring a new latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The Monfils-Schiller paradigm achieves the 'sweet spot' for extinction learning.
source: Later we describe one behavioral paradigm (the Monfils-Schiller paradigm) that achieves this sweet spot (see also Gershman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the Monfils-Schiller paradigm.

claim: Spontaneous recovery should never be complete, since the prior probability of the acquisition cause can never exceed the probability of the extinction cause.
source: One implication of this analysis is that spontaneous recovery should never be complete, since the prior probability of the acquisition cause can never exceed the probability of the extinction cause (though the ratio of probabilities increases monotonically towards one as the extinction-test interval increases); this appears generally consistent with empirical data (Rescorla, 2004).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that is consistent with empirical data.

claim: Schafe and LeDoux (2000) showed that PSI administration immediately after the acquisition of a fear memory disrupted the CR in a later test phase.
source: Schafe and LeDoux (2000) showed that PSI administration immediately after the acquisition of a fear memory disrupted the CR in a later test phase; no disruption was found if the PSI administration was delayed.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: No disruption of the CR was found if the PSI administration was delayed after acquisition.
source: Schafe and LeDoux (2000) showed that PSI administration immediately after the acquisition of a fear memory disrupted the CR in a later test phase; no disruption was found if the PSI administration was delayed.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Nader et al. (2000) showed that re-exposing the animal to the CS prior to delayed PSI administration resulted in disrupted CR.
source: However, Nader et al. (2000) showed that re-exposing the animal to the CS prior to delayed PSI administration resulted in disrupted CR.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: The reexposure failed to produce disruption if the PSI administration was delayed relative to the reexposure.
source: The reexposure failed to produce this disruption if the PSI administration was delayed relative to the reexposure.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: The model correctly predicts that PSI administration will be ineffective when delayed after acquisition.
source: These observations are reproduced by simulations of our model (Figure 4). The key idea is that the latent cause inferred during the acquisition phase has high probability only after CS exposure (either during acquisition itself or after reexposure). Since we hypothesize that PSIs disrupt the associative weights tied to latent causes in proportion to their posterior probability (i.e., their degree of 'activation'), the model correctly predicts that PSI administration will be ineffective when delayed.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that matches empirical data, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: As US variance (σ²) increases, sensitivity to the post-retrieval prediction error decreases, thereby reducing the probability that a new latent cause will be inferred.
source: As σ2 increases, sensitivity to the post-retrieval prediction error decreases, thereby reducing the probability that a new latent cause will be inferred; this effect manifests as a reduced CR at test.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about parameter effects, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: The concentration parameter has a complex effect on the CR at test: increasing α initially increases the CR at test by increasing the probability that the post-retrieval trial is assigned to a new latent cause, but then decreases the CR at test for sufficiently high values of α.
source: The concentration parameter has a more complex effect on the results: increasing α initially increases the CR at test by increasing the probability that the post-retrieval trial is assigned to a new latent cause, but then decreases the CR at test due to the fact that—for sufficiently high values of α—the test trial itself is assigned to an entirely new latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about parameter effects, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Young animals and animals with hippocampal lesions should show stronger retrieval effects.
source: Thus, these animals should show stronger retrieval effects.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the model and prior work.

claim: Eisenberg et al. (2003) found that administering a PSI after a single reexposure to the CS caused retrograde amnesia for the reactivated fear memory.
source: Using fear conditioning in the Medaka fish, Eisenberg et al. (2003) found that administering a PSI after a single reexposure to the CS (i.e., a single extinction trial) caused retrograde amnesia for the reactivated fear memory.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Administering a PSI after multiple reexposures caused retrograde amnesia for the extinction memory: high recovery of fear was observed in a test on the following day.
source: In contrast, administering the PSI after multiple reexposures caused retrograde amnesia for the extinction memory: high recovery of fear was observed in a test on the following day.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Similar results to Eisenberg et al. (2003) have been obtained with mice, rats, and the crab Chasmagnathus.
source: Similar results have been obtained with mice (Suzuki et al., 2004), rats (Lee et al., 2006a), and the crab Chasmagnathus (Pedreira and Maldonado, 2003).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from cited studies.

claim: Limited reexposure (operationalized by a single CS presentation) favors assignment of the reexposure trial to the acquisition latent cause.
source: This is also seen in our theory: limited reexposure (operationalized by a single CS presentation) favors assignment of the reexposure trial to the acquisition latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: With more trials of extinction, persistent prediction errors accrue, favoring assignment of these trials to a new latent cause.
source: However, with more trials of extinction (e.g., two or more CS presentations), persistent prediction errors accrue, favoring assignment of these trials to a new latent cause (the 'extinction' cause).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: Suzuki et al. (2004) demonstrated that the amnestic effects of PSI injection were more pronounced for young memories (i.e., short intervals between acquisition and reexposure).
source: By manipulating the interval between acquisition and reexposure, Suzuki et al. (2004) demonstrated that the amnestic effects of PSI injection were more pronounced for young memories (i.e., short intervals).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Winters et al. (2009) found a similar effect with the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 administered prior to reexposure.
source: Winters et al. (2009) found a similar effect with the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 administered prior to reexposure, and Milekic and Alberini (2002) demonstrated this effect in an inhibitory avoidance paradigm.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Milekic and Alberini (2002) demonstrated the age-dependence of reconsolidation in an inhibitory avoidance paradigm.
source: Winters et al. (2009) found a similar effect with the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 administered prior to reexposure, and Milekic and Alberini (2002) demonstrated this effect in an inhibitory avoidance paradigm.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Old observations are less likely (under the prior) to have been generated by the same latent cause as recent observations.
source: These findings can also be explained by our model: old observations are less likely (under the prior) to have been generated by the same latent cause as recent observations.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the model's prior.

claim: There is an inductive bias against modifying old memory traces.
source: Thus, there is an inductive bias against modifying old memory traces.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the model's behavior.

claim: Suzuki et al. (2004) showed that strong memories are more resistant to updating.
source: In another experiment, Suzuki et al. (2004) showed that strong memories are more resistant to updating (see also Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from cited studies.

claim: Increasing the number of acquisition trials led to persistent fear even after reexposure to the CS and PSI injection.
source: Specifically, increasing the number of acquisition trials led to persistent fear even after reexposure to the CS and PSI injection.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: For stronger memories, because the associative weight is large, the prediction error is large, which causes the model to infer a new cause for the CS-alone trial.
source: In terms of our model, this phenomenon reflects the fact that for stronger memories, because the associative weight is large, the prediction error is large, which causes the model to infer a new cause for the CS-alone trial.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the model.

claim: Doyère et al. (2007) reported that disruption of memory by an amnestic treatment is restricted to a reactivated CS, leaving intact the CR to a non-reactivated CS that had also been paired with the US.
source: Doyère et al. (2007) reported that disruption of memory by an amnestic treatment (in this case the mitogen-activated protein kinase inhibitor U0126) is restricted to a reactivated CS, leaving intact the CR to a non-reactivated CS that had also been paired with the US (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study, illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: In the model, learning only affects the CSs associated with the current inferred latent cause.
source: This finding is explained by observing that in our model learning only affects the CSs associated with the current inferred latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the model.

claim: Debiec et al. (2013) showed that cue-specificity of reconsolidation depends on separately training the two CSs; when they are trained in compound, reactivating one CS can render the other CS labile.
source: In a recent study, Debiec et al. (2013) showed that cue-specificity of reconsolidation depends on separately training the two CSs; when they are trained in compound, reactivating one CS can render the other CS labile.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: The model reproduces the effect that when trained in compound, reactivating one CS renders the other CS vulnerable to disruption.
source: Our model reproduces this effect (Figure 7B) as in this case the compound cue is assigned to a single latent cause that generates both CSs and the US, thereby coupling the two CSs.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that matches empirical data, illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: When the same CS is reexposed twice with a relatively short (1 hr) ITI separating the presentations, PSI injection following the second presentation fails to disrupt the fear memory.
source: When the same CS is reexposed twice with a relatively short (1 hr) ITI separating the presentations, PSI injection following the second presentation fails to disrupt the fear memory (Jarome et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Jarome et al. (2012) found that increasing the ITI between retrievals (from 1 hr to 6 hr, 24 hr and 1 week) resulted in a parametric decrease of fear at test.
source: Jarome et al. (2012) found that increasing the ITI between retrievals (from 1 hr to 6 hr, 24 hr and 1 week) resulted in a parametric decrease of fear at test, suggesting that longer intervals lead to disruption of the fear trace by the PSI.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Longer ITIs reduce the probability that the two reexposures were generated by the same 'extinction' latent cause, concomitantly increasing the probability that the second reexposure was generated by the 'acquisition' latent cause.
source: This effect is predicted by our theory, due to the time-dependent prior over latent causes, which prefers assigning trials separated by a long temporal interval to different causes. As a result, longer ITIs reduce the probability that the two reexposures were generated by the same 'extinction' latent cause, concomitantly increasing the probability that the second reexposure was generated by the 'acquisition' latent cause as compared to yet another new latent cause (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that matches empirical data, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Power et al. (2006) found that post-retrieval intrahippocampal infusions of anisomycin reduced conditioned responding when rats were tested 1 day later, but responding recovered when the test was administered after six days.
source: A study by Power et al. (2006) provides a clear demonstration: Following conditioning, post-retrieval intrahippocampal infusions of the PSI anisomycin reduced conditioned responding when the rats were tested 1 day later, but responding recovered when the test was administered after sic days.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: The PSI-induced memory impairment was transient.
source: Thus, the PSI-induced memory impairment was transient (see also Lattal and Abel, 2004).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from cited studies.

claim: Recovery from amnesia occurs because the relative probability of assigning a new test observation to the acquisition cause rather than to the cause associated with the retrieval session increases over time.
source: Since the amnestic agent does not entirely eliminate the memory trace, later recovery of the fear memory occurs because the relative probability of assigning a new test observation to the acquisition cause rather than to the cause associated with the retrieval session (which was, in effect, a short extinction session) increases over time (a consequence of temporal compression by the power law kernel, as explained above).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the model.

claim: The model predicts that further increasing the retrieval-test interval will eventually result in slightly reduced responding, because of the increased probability of a new latent cause at test.
source: Interestingly, the model predicts that further increasing the retrieval-test interval will eventually result in slightly reduced responding, because of the increased probability of a new latent cause at test.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Gisquet-Verrier et al. (2015) found that administering the PSI both immediately after conditioning and immediately before test eliminated the disruptive effect.
source: As in previous studies, the authors found that post-conditioning PSI administration disrupted the CR at test; the novel twist was that administering the PSI both immediately after conditioning and immediately before test eliminated the disruptive effect.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: The state-dependent version of the latent cause theory reproduced the reversal of CR disruption by PSI administration prior to the test phase.
source: We simulated state-dependency by adding the PSI as an additional CS (Figure 10). Consistent with the experimental findings of Gisquet-Verrier et al. (2015), the state-dependent version of the latent cause theory reproduced the reversal of CR disruption by PSI administration prior to the test phase.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that matches empirical data, illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: Monfils et al. (2009) and Schiller et al. (2010) demonstrated that a single reexposure of a CS 24 hr after acquisition and 10–60 min before extinction leads to persistent reduction of fear as measured by renewal, reinstatement and spontaneous recovery tests.
source: While extinction procedures after fear conditioning are, in general, not effective in producing permanent and generalizable reduction of fear, two influential studies (Monfils et al., 2009; Schiller et al., 2010) demonstrated that a single reexposure ('retrieval trial') of a CS that had been associated with a shock, 24 hr after acquisition and 10–60 min before extinction, leads to persistent reduction of fear as measured by renewal, reinstatement and spontaneous recovery tests.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from cited studies.

claim: The Monfils-Schiller effect did not require pharmacological interventions such as PSIs, and it was evident in both rodents and humans.
source: Importantly, this effect did not require pharmacological interventions such as PSIs, and it was evident in both rodents (Monfils et al., 2009) and humans (Schiller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from cited studies.

claim: Reduction of fear in humans is still evident a year later.
source: These studies also revealed that: (1) reduction of fear in humans is still evident a year later; (2) the reduction is specific to the cue-reactivated memory; and (3) increasing the retrieval-extinction interval to 6 hr eliminates the effect.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from cited studies.

claim: The reduction of fear in the Monfils-Schiller paradigm is specific to the cue-reactivated memory.
source: These studies also revealed that: (1) reduction of fear in humans is still evident a year later; (2) the reduction is specific to the cue-reactivated memory; and (3) increasing the retrieval-extinction interval to 6 hr eliminates the effect.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from cited studies.

claim: Increasing the retrieval-extinction interval to 6 hr eliminates the Monfils-Schiller effect.
source: These studies also revealed that: (1) reduction of fear in humans is still evident a year later; (2) the reduction is specific to the cue-reactivated memory; and (3) increasing the retrieval-extinction interval to 6 hr eliminates the effect.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from cited studies.

claim: The Monfils-Schiller findings have been replicated several times in rodents and humans.
source: These findings have been replicated several times in rodents (Auchter et al., 2017; Baker et al., 2013; Clem and Huganir, 2010; Jones et al., 2013; Olshavsky et al., 2013b, 2013a; Ponnusamy et al., 2016; Rao-Ruiz et al., 2011) and humans (Agren et al., 2012; Oyarzún et al., 2012; Schiller et al., 2013; Steinfurth et al., 2014), though the generality of the paradigm remains controversial (Chan et al., 2010; Costanzi et al., 2011; Kindt and Soeter, 2013; Soeter and Kindt, 2011; Kredlow et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from cited studies.

claim: The principal salient difference between the Monfils-Schiller paradigm and regular extinction training is that in the Monfils-Schiller paradigm, the interval between the first and second extinction trials is substantially longer than the intervals between all the other trials.
source: Essentially, the principal salient difference between the Monfils-Schiller paradigm and regular extinction training is that in the Monfils-Schiller paradigm, the interval between the first and second extinction trials is substantially longer than the intervals between all the other trials.
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental design.

claim: In the Monfils-Schiller paradigm, the subject spends the retrieval-extinction interval outside the acquisition context, in its home cage.
source: Another difference (which we address later) is that in the Monfils-Schiller paradigm, the subject spends the retrieval-extinction interval outside the acquisition context, in its home cage.
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental design.

claim: In the simulations, all groups ceased responding by the end of extinction.
source: As observed experimentally, in our simulations all groups ceased responding by the end of extinction.
evidence: This is a simulation result that matches empirical observations.

claim: Both Ret-long and No Ret showed spontaneous recovery after a long extinction-test delay.
source: Both Ret-long and No Ret showed spontaneous recovery after a long extinction-test delay.
evidence: This is a simulation result, illustrated in Figure 11.

claim: In the Ret-short condition there was no spontaneous recovery of fear at test.
source: In contrast, in the Ret-short condition there was no spontaneous recovery of fear at test.
evidence: This is a simulation result, illustrated in Figure 11.

claim: The extinction trials were assigned to a new latent cause in the No Ret and Ret-long conditions, but to the acquisition cause in the Ret-short condition.
source: Examining the posterior distributions over latent causes in the different conditions (Figure 11B–D), we see that the extinction trials were assigned to a new latent cause in the No Ret and Ret-long conditions, but to the acquisition cause in the Ret-short condition.
evidence: This is a simulation result, illustrated in Figure 11B-D.

claim: The theoretical explanation of the Monfils-Schiller paradigm rests critically on the 'rumination' process (i.e., iterative updating according to the EM algorithm) that occurs in the interval between the first and second extinction trials.
source: Our theoretical explanation of data from the Monfils-Schiller paradigm rests critically on the 'rumination' process (i.e., iterative updating according to the EM algorithm) that occurs in the interval between the first and second extinction trials (the REI).
evidence: This is a core theoretical claim about the mechanism underlying the Monfils-Schiller effect.

claim: The first iteration of associative learning in the EM algorithm will reduce the CS-US association for the acquisition latent cause.
source: Since there is some probability that the original ('acquisition') latent cause is active during the REI, the first iteration of associative learning in the EM algorithm will reduce the CS-US association for that latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the dynamics during the REI.

claim: On the next iteration, the model will be even more likely to infer that the original latent cause is active (since the CS-US association strength is smaller, the prediction error induced by the CS appearing without the US will be even smaller).
source: On the next iteration, the model will be even more likely to infer that the original latent cause is active (since the CS-US association strength is smaller, the prediction error induced by the CS appearing without the US will be even smaller).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the dynamics during the REI.

claim: As a result of the increased probability that the original latent cause is active, the CS-US association will be reduced even more.
source: As a result of this increased probability that the original latent cause is active, the CS-US association will be reduced even more.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the dynamics during the REI.

claim: The number of EM iterations (up to a maximum of 3 iterations) depends on the length of the REI.
source: In our model, the number of EM iterations (up to a maximum of 3 iterations, with one iteration per timestep; see model description) depends on the length of the REI.
evidence: This is a modeling choice.

claim: More iterations cause the original association to be further weakened after the first retrieval trial, and therefore spontaneous recovery of the original fear memory at test is attenuated.
source: More iterations cause the original association to be further weakened after the first retrieval trial, and therefore spontaneous recovery of the original fear memory at test is attenuated (Figure 12A).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction, illustrated in Figure 12A.

claim: When the interval is too short, there is insufficient time to reduce the CS-US association and thus later extinction trials are preferentially assigned to a new latent cause rather than the acquisition cause.
source: When the interval is too short (as in the No Ret condition), there is insufficient time (i.e., only a single EM iteration) to reduce the CS-US association and thus later extinction trials are preferentially assigned to a new latent cause rather than the acquisition cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the No Ret condition.

claim: When the interval is too long, although the CS-US association of the acquisition latent cause is reduced during the REI, extinction trials will be preferentially assigned to a new latent cause due to the time-sensitive prior.
source: When the interval is too long (as in the Ret-long condition), although the CS-US association of the acquisition latent cause is reduced during the REI, extinction trials will be preferentially assigned to a new latent cause due to the time-sensitive prior that suggests that events far away in time are generated by different causes.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the Ret-long condition.

claim: It is only in the intermediate condition, the short REI, that the EM iterations reduce the prediction of the US by the acquisition latent cause sufficiently so as to allow later extinction trials to be assigned to this same latent cause.
source: It is only in the intermediate condition, the short REI, that the EM iterations reduce the prediction of the US by the acquisition latent cause sufficiently so as to allow later extinction trials to be assigned to this same latent cause, therefore reducing the prediction of the US by this cause even further, effectively 'erasing' the fear memory.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the Ret-short condition.

claim: The model predicts that all the boundary conditions discussed earlier should apply to the Monfils-Schiller paradigm.
source: Note that our model predicts that all the boundary conditions discussed earlier should apply to the Monfils-Schiller paradigm.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: Older memories should be more difficult to disrupt, even with an intermediate REI.
source: Thus, for example, older memories should be more difficult to disrupt, even with an intermediate REI.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: The theory predicts that distracting or occupying animals during the interval should disrupt the Monfils-Schiller effect.
source: The importance of iterative adjustment during the retrieval-extinction interval suggests that distracting or occupying animals during the interval should disrupt the Monfils-Schiller effect.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: Giving rodents a secondary task to perform during the interval will prevent the iterative weakening of the CS-US association of the acquisition cause, leading to assignment of extinction trials to a new latent cause and to later recovery of fear.
source: For example, our theory predicts that giving rodents a secondary task to perform during the interval will prevent the iterative weakening of the CS-US association of the acquisition cause, leading to assignment of extinction trials to a new latent cause (as in regular extinction) and to later recovery of fear.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: Schiller et al. (2010) found that fear recovered for the CS that was not reexposed, but not for the reexposed CS.
source: Consistent with the findings of Doyère et al. (2007), Schiller et al. (2010) found that fear recovered for the CS that was not reexposed, but not for the reexposed CS.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: CS reexposure leads to memory modification for the US association specific to that CS and the reactivated latent cause.
source: This finding fits with our theoretical interpretation that CS reexposure leads to memory modification for the US association specific to that CS and the reactivated latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of empirical findings.

claim: Several studies have failed to show persistent reduction of fear using the Monfils-Schiller paradigm.
source: Several studies have failed to show persistent reduction of fear using the Monfils-Schiller paradigm (Chan et al., 2010; Costanzi et al., 2011; Kindt and Soeter, 2013; Soeter and Kindt, 2011).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from cited studies.

claim: Costanzi et al. (2011) trained mice to associate a foot-shock with a context, and then induced retrieval of the contextual memory 29 days later.
source: Costanzi et al. (2011) trained mice to associate a foot-shock with a context, and then induced retrieval of the contextual memory 29 days later by placing the mice in the conditioning context for 3 min.
evidence: This is a description of an experimental procedure from a cited study.

claim: Costanzi et al. (2011) found that extinction after retrieval did not attenuate contextual fear any more so than regular extinction without a retrieval trial.
source: Costanzi et al. (2011) found that extinction after retrieval did not attenuate contextual fear any more so than regular extinction without a retrieval trial, contrary to the findings of Monfils et al. (2009).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: A crucial difference between the studies of Costanzi et al. (2011) and Monfils et al. (2009) was the acquisition-retrieval interval: 29 days in Costanzi et al. (2011) and 1 day in Monfils et al. (2009).
source: Auber et al. (2013) pointed out that a crucial difference between the studies of Costanzi et al. (2011) and Monfils et al. (2009) was the acquisition-retrieval interval: 29 days in Costanzi et al. (2011) and 1 day in Monfils et al. (2009).
evidence: This is an observation from a cited study.

claim: When the acquisition-retrieval interval is long, the retrieval trial is less likely to have been generated by the same latent cause as the acquisition trials.
source: According to our theory, this phenomenon occurs because when the acquisition-retrieval interval is long, the retrieval trial is less likely to have been generated by the same latent cause as the acquisition trials.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the model.

claim: The theory predicts the difference between the Costanzi et al. (2011) and Monfils et al. (2009) experiments.
source: Our theory therefore predicts the difference between the two experiments (Figure 14A).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction, illustrated in Figure 14A.

claim: Gräff et al. (2014) found that younger memories were more susceptible to modification.
source: A direct comparison of new and old memories in the Monfils-Schiller paradigm was reported by (Gräff et al., 2014); consistent with our hypothesis, younger memories were more susceptible to modification (see also Jones and Monfils, 2016, for converging evidence).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Chan et al. (2010) found that the Monfils-Schiller paradigm failed to prevent the return of fear in renewal and reinstatement tests.
source: In another study reporting discrepant results, Chan et al. (2010) found that the Monfils-Schiller paradigm failed to prevent the return of fear in renewal and reinstatement tests.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Chan et al. (2010) used different experimental boxes located in different rooms for acquisition and for retrieval and extinction, whereas Monfils et al. (2009) modified the conditioning box to create a new context for retrieval and extinction, while keeping the room the same.
source: Auber et al. (2013) observed that the study by Chan et al. (2010) used different experimental boxes located in different rooms for acquisition and for retrieval and extinction, whereas in their renewal experiment Monfils et al. (2009) modified the conditioning box to create a new context for retrieval and extinction, while keeping the room the same.
evidence: This is an observation from a cited study.

claim: Retrieval and extinction in a similar context led to less renewal at test than did retrieval and extinction in a very different context.
source: We found that retrieval and extinction in a similar context led to less renewal at test than did retrieval and extinction in a very different context (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is a simulation result, illustrated in Figure 14B.

claim: When acquisition and retrieval/extinction contexts are similar, there is a higher probability that the latter trials will be assigned to the original acquisition latent cause.
source: This is because when acquisition and retrieval/extinction contexts are similar, there is a higher probability that the latter trials will be assigned to the original acquisition latent cause—i.e., that the 'retrieval' trial will indeed retrieve the old association (see also Gershman et al., 2010, 2013c).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the model.

claim: Retrieval without extinction leads to 'paradoxical' enhancement of a weak acquisition memory at the time of test.
source: It has been observed that retrieval without extinction leads to 'paradoxical' enhancement of a weak acquisition memory at the time of test (Eysenck, 1968; Rohrbaugh and Riccio, 1970; Rohrbaugh et al., 1972).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from cited studies.

claim: Paradoxical enhancement of memory may be related to well-established 'testing effects', which show that memory is enhanced by the act of retrieval even in the absence of feedback.
source: Paradoxical enhancement of memory may be related to well-established 'testing effects', which show that memory is enhanced by the act of retrieval even in the absence of feedback (e.g., Karpicke and Roediger, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical connection to prior work.

claim: There is evidence that paradoxical enhancement is transient, disappearing with longer retrieval-test intervals.
source: There is also evidence that paradoxical enhancement is transient, disappearing with longer retrieval-test intervals (Gisquet-Verrier and Alexinsky, 1990).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from a cited study.

claim: The retrieval trial induces the inference that the acquisition cause is once again active, and this inference persists into the test phase due to the contiguity principle.
source: Our model accounts for these findings (Figure 15) by positing that the retrieval trial induces the inference that the acquisition cause is once again active, and this inference persists into the test phase due to the contiguity principle.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation, illustrated in Figure 15.

claim: The role of the retrieval trial in the theory is to 'bridge the gap' between training and test, and prolong the duration for which the acquisition cause is inferred to be active.
source: That is, when comparing to a test phase without the retrieval trial, the role of the retrieval trial in our theory is to 'bridge the gap' between training and test, and prolong the duration for which the acquisition cause is inferred to be active.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation.

claim: The paradoxical enhancement of memory due to retrieval can be explained by the model in terms of altered retrieval probability rather than new associative learning.
source: The paradoxical enhancement of memory due to retrieval can thus be explained by our model in terms of altered retrieval probability rather than new associative learning.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation.

claim: The model makes predictions regarding the efficacy of the retrieval trial as a function of its delay after conditioning—delayed retrieval just before test should be less effective at enhancing fear at test.
source: Our model makes further predictions regarding the efficacy of the retrieval trial as a function of its delay after conditioning—delayed retrieval just before test should be less effective at enhancing fear at test, because it is less likely to reactivate the acquisition latent cause.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the model.

claim: Major phenomena in post-retrieval memory modification can be accounted for by a rational analysis of Pavlovian conditioning.
source: We have shown how major phenomena in post-retrieval memory modification can be accounted for by a rational analysis of Pavlovian conditioning.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the paper's contributions.

claim: The key idea of the theory is a distinction between two learning processes: a structure learning process that infers the latent causes underlying sensory data, and an associative learning process that adjusts the parameters of the internal model.
source: The key idea of our theory is a distinction between two learning processes: a structure learning process that infers the latent causes underlying sensory data, and an associative learning process that adjusts the parameters of the internal model so that each latent cause is likely to give rise to the sensory data ascribed to it.
evidence: This is a summary of the core theoretical contribution.

claim: The theory formalizes the dynamic interplay between learning and memory, which is at the heart of post-retrieval memory modification phenomena.
source: The main difference is that our theory extends previous associative learning theories that concentrate on the latter process while assuming a fixed model of the environment, and formalizes the dynamic interplay between learning and memory, which we suggest is at the heart of post-retrieval memory modification phenomena.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical contribution.

claim: The theory can reproduce experimentally observed boundary conditions on memory modification, such as the effects of age, memory strength, and prediction error.
source: We further show that the theory can reproduce experimentally observed boundary conditions on memory modification, such as the effects of age, memory strength, and prediction error.
evidence: This is a summary of the paper's contributions.

claim: The Monfils-Schiller paradigm is theoretically tantalizing because it is not a priori clear what is the difference between the retrieval trial and the first trial of any extinction session.
source: The Monfils-Schiller paradigm is theoretically tantalizing because it is not a priori clear what is the difference between the retrieval trial and the first trial of any extinction session—why is it that the CS-alone trial in the Monfils-Schiller paradigm acts as a 'retrieval cue', while the first CS-alone trial of a regular extinction session does not?
evidence: This is a theoretical puzzle that the paper addresses.

claim: The theory resolves the puzzle of the Monfils-Schiller paradigm by stressing the role of the extended period of learning during the long retrieval-extinction gap.
source: Our theory resolves this puzzle by stressing the role of the extended period of learning (in our model, additional iterations of the EM algorithm) during the long retrieval-extinction gap, in which the rat is left in its home cage to 'ruminate' about its recent experience.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical explanation for the Monfils-Schiller paradigm.

claim: The explanation rests not on the existence of a separate reconsolidation process, but rather on the same learning and memory mechanisms that are at play in acquisition and extinction.
source: Thus our explanation rests not on the existence of a separate reconsolidation process that is invoked by the retrieval trial, but rather on the same learning and memory mechanisms that are at play in acquisition and extinction—the idea that inference about the latent structure of the environment affects whether new information will update an old association, or whether it will be attributed to a new memory (new latent cause).
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical explanation.

claim: According to the theory, the 'retrieval' trial is not different from any other trial, and perhaps a more accurate nomenclature would be to call the retrieval-extinction interval an 'updating interval'.
source: In this sense, according to our theory, the 'retrieval' trial is, in fact, not different from any other trial, and perhaps a more accurate nomenclature would be to call the retrieval-extinction interval an 'updating interval' rather than focus on a 'retrieval cue'.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Monfils et al. (2009) reported increased phosphorylation of AMPA receptors in the lateral amygdala after the retrieval trial.
source: Monfils et al. (2009) reported increased phosphorylation of AMPA receptors in the lateral amygdala after the retrieval trial (a possible correlate of memory labilization), and also found that a second CS presented one hour after the first reversed the increase in AMPAr phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Clem and Huganir (2010) found that extinction following retrieval resulted in synaptic removal of calcium-permeable AMPA receptors.
source: Clem and Huganir (2010) found that extinction following retrieval resulted in synaptic removal of calcium-permeable AMPA receptors.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: The Monfils-Schiller paradigm has been shown to induce neural modifications that are distinct from standard extinction.
source: Furthermore, the Monfils-Schiller paradigm has been shown to induce neural modifications that are distinct from standard extinction (Lee et al., 2015; Tedesco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from cited studies.

claim: During the retrieval-extinction interval, an associative learning process is engaged that decrements the CS-US association.
source: We showed in simulations that during the retrieval-extinction interval, an associative learning process is engaged (and continues to be engaged during extinction training) that decrements the CS-US association, whereas in our model standard extinction engages a structure learning process that assigns the extinction trials to a new latent cause, creating a new memory trace without modifying the original memory.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on simulation results.

claim: In the model, standard extinction engages a structure learning process that assigns the extinction trials to a new latent cause, creating a new memory trace without modifying the original memory.
source: We showed in simulations that during the retrieval-extinction interval, an associative learning process is engaged (and continues to be engaged during extinction training) that decrements the CS-US association, whereas in our model standard extinction engages a structure learning process that assigns the extinction trials to a new latent cause, creating a new memory trace without modifying the original memory.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on simulation results.

claim: The hippocampus is a key brain region involved in partitioning streams of experience into latent causes.
source: In previous work, we have suggested that the hippocampus is a key brain region involved in partitioning streams of experience into latent causes (Gershman et al., 2010, 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from prior work.

claim: Context-specific memories depend on the integrity of the hippocampus.
source: Some of the evidence for this view comes from studies showing that context-specific memories depend on the integrity of the hippocampus (e.g., Honey and Good, 1993), indicating that animals without a hippocampus cannot 'carve nature at its joints' (i.e., partition observations into latent causes; see Gershman and Niv, 2010; Gershman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from cited studies, with a theoretical interpretation.

claim: The dentate gyrus activates latent representations of the sensory inputs in area CA3.
source: Within the current model, we propose that the dentate gyrus (DG) activates latent representations of the sensory inputs in area CA3.
evidence: This is a proposed neural implementation.

claim: Each latent representation in CA3 corresponds to a latent cause, and their level of activation is proportional to their prior probability.
source: Each of these representations corresponds to a latent cause, and their level of activation is proportional to their prior probability (Equation 3).
evidence: This is a proposed neural implementation.

claim: Latent cause representations may be encoded in attractors by the dense recurrent collaterals that are characteristic of CA3.
source: Mechanistically, these representations may be encoded in attractors by the dense recurrent collaterals that are characteristic of CA3 (McNaughton and Morris, 1987).
evidence: This is a proposed neural mechanism, with a citation to prior work.

claim: One potential mechanism for creating new attractors is neurogenesis of granule cells in the DG.
source: One potential mechanism for creating new attractors is neurogenesis of granule cells in the DG (Becker, 2005).
evidence: This is a proposed neural mechanism, with a citation to prior work.

claim: The role of neurogenesis in creating new attractors should be time-sensitive in a manner comparable to the latent cause prior.
source: This account predicts that the role of neurogenesis in creating new attractors should be time-sensitive in a manner comparable to the latent cause prior (i.e., it should implement the contiguity principle).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about neural mechanisms.

claim: Immature granule cells, by virtue of their low activation thresholds, high resting potentials and constant turnover, cause inputs that are distant in time to map onto distinct CA3 representations.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, Aimone et al. (2006) have suggested that immature granule cells, by virtue of their low activation thresholds, high resting potentials and constant turnover, cause inputs that are distant in time to map onto distinct CA3 representations.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from a cited study.

claim: New granule cells die over time if they are not involved in new learning.
source: Furthermore, evidence suggests that new granule cells die over time if they are not involved in new learning (Shors et al., 2012), offering another mechanism by which the contiguity principle could be implemented.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from a cited study, with a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Suppression of neurogenesis reduces both behavioral and neural discrimination between similar contexts.
source: Consistent with the idea that neurogenesis supports the partitioning of experience into latent causes, suppression of neurogenesis reduces both behavioral and neural discrimination between similar contexts (Niibori et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Many CA3 neurons are temporally selective, responding to individual contexts only if exposures are separated by long temporal intervals, and this selectivity depends on intact neurogenesis.
source: Importantly, many CA3 neurons are temporally selective, responding to individual contexts only if exposures are separated by long temporal intervals, and this selectivity depends on intact neurogenesis (Rangel et al., 2014), as one would expect based on the contiguity principle.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study, with a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Suppression of neurogenesis will force experiences separated by long temporal gaps to be assigned to the same latent cause, thus eliminating the age-based boundary condition on memory modification.
source: Our interpretation of neurogenesis predicts that its suppression (e.g., by irradiation of the DG), will force experiences separated by long temporal gaps to be assigned to the same latent cause, thus eliminating the age-based boundary condition on memory modification (Alberini, 2007; Milekic and Alberini, 2002; Suzuki et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the proposed neural implementation.

claim: CS-US associations in auditory fear conditioning are encoded by synapses between the thalamus and the basolateral amygdala.
source: There is widespread agreement that CS-US associations in auditory fear conditioning are encoded by synapses between the thalamus and the basolateral amygdala (BLA; McNally et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a claim about the neural substrate, supported by a citation.

claim: The amygdala transmits a US prediction that is then compared to sensory afferents from the periacqueductal gray region of the midbrain.
source: Accordingly, we suggest that the amygdala transmits a US prediction that is then compared to sensory afferents from the periacqueductal gray region of the midbrain.
evidence: This is a proposed neural implementation.

claim: The resultant prediction error is computed in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and transmitted by dopaminergic projections to both the amygdala and CA1.
source: The resultant prediction error is computed in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and transmitted by dopaminergic projections to both the amygdala and CA1.
evidence: This is a proposed neural implementation.

claim: The theory makes the testable prediction that disrupting the neural substrates of associative learning during the retrieval-extinction interval should block memory updating in the Monfils-Schiller paradigm.
source: Our theory makes the testable prediction that disrupting the neural substrates of associative learning, or potentiating the neural substrates responsible for inferring new latent causes, during the retrieval-extinction interval should block memory updating in the Monfils-Schiller paradigm.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the proposed neural implementation.

claim: Deactivating the BLA or stimulating the DG should block memory updating following retrieval.
source: Thus, both deactivating the BLA or stimulating the DG (e.g., using optogenetic manipulations) should block memory updating following retrieval.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the proposed neural implementation.

claim: The relative balance of activity in the BLA and DG should relate to individual differences in conditional responding in the test phase.
source: We also predict that the relative balance of activity in these two regions, measured for example using fMRI, should relate to individual differences in conditional responding in the test phase.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the proposed neural implementation.

claim: The role of dopamine in associative learning is well established.
source: The role of dopamine in associative learning is well established (see Glimcher, 2011 for a review), and has been specifically implicated in Pavlovian fear conditioning (Pezze and Feldon, 2004), although the role of dopamine in aversive conditioning is still a matter of controversy (Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1996; Brooks and Berns, 2013; Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about the role of dopamine, supported by citations.

claim: Dopamine gates synaptic plasticity in the basolateral amygdala.
source: Dopamine gates synaptic plasticity in the basolateral amygdala (Bissière et al., 2003), consistent with its hypothesized role in driving the learning of CS-US associations.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study, with a theoretical interpretation.

claim: Dopaminergic inputs to CA1 have a role in influencing the posterior distribution over latent causes.
source: We hypothesize that dopaminergic inputs to CA1 have an additional role: influencing the posterior distribution over latent causes.
evidence: This is a proposed neural mechanism.

claim: Dopamine prediction errors can be used to assess the similarity of current sensory inputs to those expected by the current configuration of latent causes.
source: That is, dopamine prediction errors can be used to assess the similarity of current sensory inputs to those expected by the current configuration of latent causes.
evidence: This is a proposed neural mechanism.

claim: Large discrepancies will cause the generation of a new latent cause, to account for the current unpredicted sensory input.
source: Large discrepancies will cause the generation of a new latent cause, to account for the current unpredicted sensory input (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is a proposed neural mechanism, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The output of CA1 feeds back into the VTA by way of the subiculum, potentially providing a mechanism by which the posterior distribution over latent causes can modulate the prediction errors.
source: The output of CA1 further feeds back into the VTA by way of the subiculum (Lisman and Grace, 2005), potentially providing a mechanism by which the posterior distribution over latent causes can modulate the prediction errors, as suggested by our model.
evidence: This is a proposed neural mechanism, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Reichelt et al. (2013) showed that dysregulating dopaminergic activity in the VTA prevented the destabilization of memory by NMDA receptor antagonists following a retrieval trial.
source: In appetitive conditioning experiments, (Reichelt et al., 2013) have shown that dysregulating dopaminergic activity in the VTA prevented the destabilization of memory by NMDA receptor antagonists (injected systemically following a retrieval trial), consistent with the hypothesis that dopaminergic prediction errors are necessary for memory updating after memory retrieval.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study, with a theoretical interpretation.

claim: A key claim of this paper is that associative and structure learning are coupled: learning about associations depends on structural inferences, and vice versa.
source: A key claim of this paper is that associative and structure learning are coupled: learning about associations depends on structural inferences, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a summary of a core theoretical claim.
